Shared predictive importance with sharedimp

Source: vignettes/sharedimp.Rmd
sharedimp.Rmd

sharedimp implements the linear-regression variant of ultra-marginal feature importance (UMFI-LR; Janssen, Guan and Robeva, AISTATS 2023) in a form that fits modern resampling-based workflows. The package does not introduce a new importance measure. It makes an existing one safe to use: the residualization step is estimated inside each training fold, the two models being compared are evaluated on the same assessment rows, the sign of the result does not depend on the metric, and negative values are not hidden.

The idea in one paragraph

Take an anchor feature XiX_i. Regress every other feature XjX_j on XiX_i (ordinary least squares with an intercept) and keep the residuals Rj=Xj−aj−bjXiR_j = X_j - a_j - b_j X_i. By construction the residuals are uncorrelated with the anchor on the data used to fit them. Now compare two models of yy:

  • full: [Xi,R−i][X_i, R_{-i}] — the anchor plus the residualized others;
  • reduced: [R−i][R_{-i}] — the residualized others only.

The out-of-sample gain of the full model over the reduced model is the importance of XiX_i. Because the linear part of XiX_i has been removed from the other features, information that XiX_ishares with correlated features is credited to XiX_i rather than being split or lost, which is what distinguishes UMFI from ablation and permutation importance for correlated predictors.

A worked example 

library(sharedimp)
set.seed(2026)
n <- 300
x <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n),
  x2 = rnorm(n),
  x3 = rnorm(n),
  x4 = rnorm(n)
)
x$x5 <- x$x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2) # a noisy copy of x1
y <- 3 * x$x1 + 2 * x$x2 + 1 * x$x3 + rnorm(n)

x4 is pure noise and x5 is a near-duplicate of x1. With the fast, deterministic linear learner and the mean squared error:

res <- shared_importance(x, y, learner = "linear", v = 5, seed = 1)
res
#> <sharedimp_result>
#>   task:       regression
#>   learner:    linear
#>   metric:     mse (minimize); importance = -(full - reduced)
#>   resampling: 5-fold cross-validation (1 repeat)
#> 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   feature importance     sd n_folds
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 x1          9.81   1.41         5
#> 2 x2          6.67   0.572        5
#> 3 x3          1.38   0.352        5
#> 4 x4          0.0742 0.0793       5
#> 5 x5          9.58   1.38         5

Importance is -(MSE_full - MSE_reduced), i.e. the increase in MSE caused by dropping the anchor while keeping the residualized others. For an independent linear-Gaussian design it is approximately βi2Var(Xi)\beta_i^2 \mathrm{Var}(X_i): roughly 9, 4 and 1 for x1, x2, x3, and 0 for the noise feature. The near-duplicate x5 receives almost the same importance as x1: once x1 is residualized on x5, little of x1 is left, so x5 carries the shared signal. This is the duplication-symmetry property of UMFI.

The per-fold paired metrics are always kept:

fold_results(res)
#> # A tibble: 25 × 7
#>    feature id    id2   metric_full metric_reduced importance error
#>    <chr>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>
#>  1 x1      Fold1 NA          1.29           10.1        8.82 NA   
#>  2 x1      Fold2 NA          1.04           12.2       11.2  NA   
#>  3 x1      Fold3 NA          0.708          10.0        9.32 NA   
#>  4 x1      Fold4 NA          1.03            9.35       8.32 NA   
#>  5 x1      Fold5 NA          0.904          12.3       11.4  NA   
#>  6 x2      Fold1 NA          1.29            8.36       7.08 NA   
#>  7 x2      Fold2 NA          1.04            7.34       6.31 NA   
#>  8 x2      Fold3 NA          0.708           6.90       6.20 NA   
#>  9 x2      Fold4 NA          1.03            8.50       7.48 NA   
#> 10 x2      Fold5 NA          0.904           7.20       6.30 NA   
#> # ℹ 15 more rows

Negative fold values for x4 are expected and are reported as they are.

Choosing the learner and the metric

The default learner is a random forest (ranger, 500 trees, min_n = 5) with fixed hyperparameters. Any parsnip model specification can be used instead, as can a pair of fit/predict functions wrapped with sharedimp_learner().

res_rf <- shared_importance(x, y, v = 5, seed = 1)
res_rf$importance
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   feature importance     sd n_folds
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 x1           9.23  1.95         5
#> 2 x2           6.37  0.823        5
#> 3 x3           1.01  0.345        5
#> 4 x4          -0.124 0.0872       5
#> 5 x5           9.05  1.81         5

Metrics come from yardstick. The direction attribute of the metric decides the sign convention, so a metric to maximize ("rsq", "accuracy", "roc_auc") and a metric to minimize ("mse", "rmse", "mae", "mn_log_loss") both yield positive importance when the anchor helps.

shared_importance(x, y, learner = "linear", metric = "rsq", v = 5, seed = 1)$importance
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   feature importance      sd n_folds
#>   <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 x1         0.572   0.107         5
#> 2 x2         0.419   0.118         5
#> 3 x3         0.0897  0.0379        5
#> 4 x4         0.00595 0.00664       5
#> 5 x5         0.552   0.118         5

Classification

For a factor response the task is classification. The first factor level is the event level for probability metrics, and folds are stratified by y.

yb <- factor(ifelse(y > median(y), "high", "low"), levels = c("high", "low"))
res_b <- shared_importance(x, yb, learner = "linear", metric = "mn_log_loss", v = 5, seed = 1)
#> Warning: The learner emitted 16 warning(s) during fitting or prediction:
#> • [16 times] glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
res_b$importance
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   feature importance     sd n_folds
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 x1          0.406  0.129        5
#> 2 x2          0.329  0.134        5
#> 3 x3          0.0792 0.0372       5
#> 4 x4         -0.0174 0.0444       5
#> 5 x5          0.400  0.144        5

Multiclass responses work the same way; "roc_auc" then uses the Hand-Till estimator and "mn_log_loss" the multinomial log loss.

Reproducibility and explicit folds

seed controls fold generation and any stochastic learner under a local RNG state, leaving the caller’s random stream untouched. For comparisons across software (for example with the Python implementation of the same specification) pass explicit folds, either an rsample rset or a vector of fold labels:

labels <- rep(1:5, length.out = n)
res_fixed <- shared_importance(x, y, learner = "linear", resamples = labels)
res_fixed$resampling
#> [1] "user-supplied fold labels (5 folds)"

What the numbers are and are not

The values are out-of-sample predictive gains for a given learner, metric and resampling scheme. They are not causal effects, not conditional effects, and not regression coefficients. The sd column is the dispersion of the fold-level values and is purely descriptive; the package deliberately provides no confidence intervals or p-values.

The optional direction = TRUE diagnostic reports the correlation between the anchor and the difference between the full and reduced predictions on the assessment rows. It summarises whether the anchor’s contribution to the prediction increases or decreases with the anchor’s value and nothing more.

shared_importance(x, y, learner = "linear", v = 5, seed = 1, direction = TRUE)$importance
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   feature importance     sd n_folds direction
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 x1          9.81   1.41         5         1
#> 2 x2          6.67   0.572        5         1
#> 3 x3          1.38   0.352        5         1
#> 4 x4          0.0742 0.0793       5        -1
#> 5 x5          9.58   1.38         5         1

Relation to the reference UMFI implementation

The reference implementation (https://github.com/HydroML/UMFI) fits the residualization on the whole data set, gates it on a slope p-value, scores random forests by out-of-bag R2R^2 or accuracy with floors, and sets negative values to zero. sharedimp residualizes inside each training fold, always residualizes, uses paired per-fold assessment metrics with any learner, and keeps negative values. Numerical identity is therefore not expected; the specification and a recorded comparison are in the docs/ directory of the source repository.
